### Kingfisher and roses 
China, Qing dynasty (1644-1911), 18th century
Kori (silk tapestry), hanging scroll, 84 x 39.5 cm
Seal mark: Mriyi yansans
Gift of Dr Lam Kwok Pun
HKUT.2008.1679 
Woven on a beige background, this bird, likely a kingfisher with its iconic blue feathers, holds fruit in its mouth and rests on the branch of a rose bush. The greyish-blue feathers are woven with the longfinch-gazing ('long-and-short) propinquity; technique, and the gradation of dark grey feathers on its wing are achieved using the grain ('flinging') technique. As the weft threads were woven horizontally on looms, the gradation of colours moves from left to right, or right to left, as seen on the kingfisher's feathers. 
As roses bloom once a month, they are known as yuejiuhua or changchushua ('flowers of eternal youth'), and are traditionally symbols of longevity. A seal mark that reads neiyi yansans ('a carefree life brings longevity') in the lower right corner of the tapestry echoes this symbolic meaning. 
HKUT.2008.1679
